```{r environment-record, include = FALSE}
  n_distinct(gsub('(lme4|lmerTest) [^,]+, ', '', version_check$packages)) == 1,
  earlier_lme4$lme4 == stored_versions$lme4, earlier_lme4$lmerTest == newer_versions$lmerTest,
  library_versions(libraries[3])$lmerTest == stored_versions$lmerTest,
  n_distinct(vapply(libraries, function(l) library_versions(l)$Matrix, character(1))) == 1,
  # with the earlier lme4 the output is the stored one, and with the newer lme4
  # only its formatting differs
  all(library_rows(libraries[2])$same_output), all(library_rows(libraries[3])$same_output),
  !any(library_rows('renv.lock')$same_output), all(library_rows('renv.lock')$same_result),
  all(changes$correlated_tables > 0), all(changes$one_more_space), all(changes$uncorrelated_unchanged),
  all(changes$explained), all(changes$same_numbers), any(changes$renamed > 0), any(changes$reordered > 0),
  # and the rest of the environment differed
  earlier_lme4$System != stored_versions$System, earlier_lme4$R != stored_versions$R,
  earlier_lme4$Matrix != stored_versions$Matrix, earlier_lme4$lmerTest != stored_versions$lmerTest,
  length(other_changed) > 0,
  numeric_version(newer_versions$lme4) > numeric_version(stored_versions$lme4))
```

The session's `r count_text(nrow(executions))` stored executions ran under R `r stored_versions$R` on `r stored_system` with lme4 `r stored_versions$lme4`, lmerTest `r stored_versions$lmerTest` and Matrix `r stored_versions$Matrix`. Every script printed identical output each time, including its model summaries and warnings. `r stored_release` still distributes those versions, and [a Dockerfile](`r experiment_url('Dockerfile')`) rebuilds the environment from them, taking the other packages from the same release. Executed in that rebuild on a GitHub Actions runner, all `r count_text(nrow(verification))` scripts printed output identical to that of the stored executions, as [verification.csv](`r experiment_url('verification.csv')`) records.

```{r rerun}
# run_script_with_retries(), data_file_for() and child_environment() come from
# experiment/run_script.R, which also made the stored executions. The list of
# scripts (scripts, n_scripts) and their stored executions (stored_of()) are
# read from design.csv and executions.csv earlier on the page.
source(file.path(experiment, 'run_script.R'))

# Every script executed once more, and again if its R process crashes, which
# happens occasionally on Windows
rerun_attempts <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(n_scripts), function(i)
  run_script_with_retries(scripts$run_id[i], data_file_for(scripts$data[i]),
                          experiment_dir = normalizePath(experiment), label = 'page')))
rerun <- rerun_attempts |> group_by(run_id) |> filter(attempt == max(attempt)) |> ungroup()
rerun <- rerun[match(scripts$run_id, rerun$run_id), ]
page_environment <- child_environment()

# Rscript exits with status 1 when a script stops with an error. Any other
# nonzero status means that the R process itself ended abnormally, as when it
# crashes, which says nothing about the script.
rerun$outcome <- ifelse(rerun$status == 0, 'completed', ifelse(rerun$status == 1, 'error', 'crash'))
rerun$same_result <- rerun$outcome == 'completed' & !is.na(rerun$result) &
  rerun$result == stored_of(rerun$run_id, 'result')
rerun$same_output <- rerun$outcome == 'completed' &
  rerun$stdout_sha256 == stored_of(rerun$run_id, 'stdout_sha256')

c(stored_executions = nrow(executions), scripts = n_scripts,
  completed_now = sum(rerun$outcome == 'completed'),
  completed_after_a_crash = sum(rerun$outcome == 'completed' & rerun$attempt > 1),
  stopped_with_error_now = sum(rerun$outcome == 'error'), crashed_now = sum(rerun$outcome == 'crash'),
  same_result_now = sum(rerun$same_result), same_output_now = sum(rerun$same_output))
```

```{r rerun-text, include = FALSE}
# The wording of the paragraph below, from the counts above
n_completed <- sum(rerun$outcome == 'completed')
n_error <- sum(rerun$outcome == 'error')
n_crash <- sum(rerun$outcome == 'crash')
n_retried <- sum(rerun$outcome == 'completed' & rerun$attempt > 1)
n_same_result <- sum(rerun$same_result)
n_same_output <- sum(rerun$same_output)
# The abstract and the summary say that the scripts printed the same results
# under newer versions, so every execution that completes must print the
# stored result line, whatever its output otherwise
stopifnot(n_same_result == n_completed)

# How a crashed process ended. Windows reports an access violation as status
# -1073741819 (0xC0000005), and processx reports a Unix signal as its negative.
crash_kind <- function(status) {
  if (status == -1073741819) 'an access violation'
  else if (.Platform$OS.type == 'unix' && status < 0) sprintf('signal %d', -status)
  else sprintf('exit status %d', status)
}
crash_kinds <- knitr::combine_words(unique(vapply(rerun$status[rerun$outcome == 'crash'],
                                                  crash_kind, character(1))), and = ' or ')

completed_text <- if (n_completed == n_scripts) {
  sprintf('All %s scripts ran to completion', count_text(n_scripts))
} else {
  sprintf('Of the %s scripts, %s ran to completion', count_text(n_scripts), count_text(n_completed, n_scripts))
}
rerun_text <- if (n_same_output == n_scripts) {
  sprintf('All %s scripts printed output identical to that of the stored executions.', count_text(n_scripts))
} else if (n_completed == 0) {
  sprintf('None of the %s scripts ran to completion.', count_text(n_scripts))
} else if (n_same_output == n_completed) {
  sprintf('%s and printed output identical to that of the stored executions.', completed_text)
} else {
  sprintf('%s and printed the same result line as the stored executions, but %s printed identical output.',
          completed_text, if (n_same_output == 0) 'none' else sprintf('only %s', count_text(n_same_output, n_scripts)))
}
retry_text <- if (n_retried == 0) '' else {
  sprintf(' In %s of them, the R process crashed at first and the script completed when executed again.',
          count_text(n_retried, n_scripts))
}
failure_text <- if (n_error + n_crash == 0) {
  ''
} else if (n_crash == 0) {
  sprintf(' The other %s stopped with an error.', count_text(n_error))
} else if (n_error == 0) {
  sprintf(' In the other %s, the R process itself crashed with %s on every attempt.', count_text(n_crash), crash_kinds)
} else {
  sprintf(' Of the other %s, %s stopped with an error, and in %s the R process itself crashed with %s on every attempt.',
          count_text(n_error + n_crash), count_text(n_error), count_text(n_crash), crash_kinds)
}

# The page is knitted with the version of R and the packages that renv.lock
# (read above) pins, and the text calls them newer than those of the stored
# executions
page_versions <- versions_of(page_environment)
version_columns <- c('R', 'lme4', 'lmerTest', 'Matrix')
stopifnot(page_versions$R == lock$R$Version,
          vapply(c('lme4', 'lmerTest', 'Matrix'), function(p)
            page_versions[[p]] == lock$Packages[[p]]$Version, logical(1)),
          numeric_version(page_versions$R) > numeric_version(stored_versions$R),
          numeric_version(page_versions$lme4) > numeric_version(stored_versions$lme4),
          # the page runs in the library that check_versions.R recorded as
          # renv.lock, as the paragraph on locating the difference and Table 4 say
          unlist(page_versions[version_columns]) == unlist(newer_versions[version_columns]))
```

This page executes every script once more whenever it is knitted, under the versions of R and of the packages that the site's [renv.lock](`r sprintf('https://github.com/pablobernabeu/website-files/blob/%s/renv.lock', last_commit(file.path('..', '..', '..', 'renv.lock')))`) pins, which are newer than those of the stored executions. When the page was last knitted, the scripts ran on `r page_versions$System` under R `r page_versions$R`, with lme4 `r page_versions$lme4`, lmerTest `r page_versions$lmerTest` and Matrix `r page_versions$Matrix`. `r rerun_text``r retry_text``r failure_text`

To locate the difference, every script was executed on one `r newer_system` machine with three libraries of packages that differ only in the versions of lme4 and lmerTest. The first is the library of renv.lock, with which this page executes the scripts, the second has the stored version of lme4 and the third the stored versions of both lme4 and lmerTest. Matrix stayed at version `r newer_versions$Matrix` in all three, since version `r stored_versions$Matrix` did not compile under R `r newer_versions$R` on that machine. With the earlier lme4 and either version of lmerTest, all `r count_text(n_scripts)` scripts printed output identical to that of the stored executions (Table 4). The rebuild of the stored environment and the library with the earlier lme4 differed in the operating system, in their linear-algebra libraries and in the versions of `r knitr::combine_words(c('R', 'Matrix', 'lmerTest', other_changed), and = ' and ', oxford_comma = FALSE)`, as well as of nloptr and other packages that lme4 depends on. Since both printed the stored output, none of those differences changed it.

The difference therefore came from the update of lme4, which changed the formatting of every script's output but none of its numbers. In every printed table of random effects with a column of correlations, each line gained one trailing space. The newer lme4 also renamed the `deviance` column of its likelihood-ratio tests to `-2*log(L)` in `r count_text(sum(changes$renamed > 0))` scripts, and in `r count_text(sum(changes$reordered > 0))` it printed the variances of the random effects before their standard deviations.

```{r environments}
labels <- c(`renv.lock` = 'Newer (renv.lock)', `lme4 1.1-35.1` = 'Newer, with lme4 as stored',
            `lme4 1.1-35.1 and lmerTest 3.1-3` = 'Newer, with lme4 and lmerTest as stored')
count_of <- function(k, n) sprintf('%d of %d', k, n)
row_of <- function(label, system, versions, same_output, same_result) {
  data.frame(Environment = label, `Operating system` = system, versions[, c('R', 'lme4', 'lmerTest', 'Matrix')],
             `Identical output` = count_of(sum(same_output), length(same_output)),
             `Same result line` = count_of(sum(same_result), length(same_result)), check.names = FALSE)
}
environment_table <- bind_rows(
  row_of('Stored, rebuilt with Docker', rebuild_release, versions_of(unique(verification$environment)),
         verification$identical, verification$result == stored_of(verification$run_id, 'result')),
  bind_rows(lapply(names(labels), function(library) {
    rows <- library_rows(library)
    row_of(labels[[library]], newer_system, library_versions(library), rows$same_output, rows$same_result)
  })))

knitr::kable(environment_table,
  caption = sprintf(paste(
    'Output of the Agents\' Scripts in %s Environments, Compared With the Stored Executions.',
    'Each script was executed once in each environment. \'Identical output\' counts the scripts whose',
    'output matched the stored output line for line, and \'Same result line\' counts those whose final',
    'line, which gives the estimate and the interval, matched.'),
    stringr::str_to_title(count_text(nrow(environment_table)))),
  align = c('l', 'l', 'r', 'r', 'r', 'r', 'r', 'r'))
```

## Discussion

The first two parts of the discussion take up the two questions of the introduction, and the last two outline a workflow and the limits of the experiment.

### What Executing Code Contributed

No text in this experiment was repeated, yet every executed script printed the same output each time the session ran it, as saved code in a fixed environment should. Because the versions of R, lme4, lmerTest and Matrix were recorded and can still be installed, a rebuild of that environment on another machine, with the other packages taken from `r stored_release`, printed the same output. Under newer versions, the only change, in formatting, disappeared when the recorded version of lme4 was restored.

The agreement between runs is a separate matter. On balanced data, the prose replies were as consistent as the scripts, and the open request was answered as consistently as the specified one, so the consistency came from the model and the task. The specified request decided which interval the runs agreed on. The executed scripts added exactness and a record that can be checked. On unbalanced data, where the model has to be fitted numerically, every script returned the exact result and each prose reply an approximation. Even where the prose replies matched the scripts, only recomputing their quantities in R could tell a correct reply from a confident error.

The results also qualify the studies reviewed above, which found large variation from one request to the next in code generation and in benchmark accuracy (Atıl et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2025). Many-analysts studies find wide variation among human analysts too. When 29 teams analysed one data set to answer one question, their odds ratios ranged from 0.89 to 2.93, and 20 of the 29 teams found a statistically significant effect (Silberzahn et al., 2018). When 70 teams tested the same hypotheses on one neuroimaging data set, no two chose the same workflow (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020). Coding agents can show the same diversity. Autonomous AI analysts given one data set and one hypothesis reached divergent verdicts in three domains, and their conclusions shifted with the model and the prompt (Bertran et al., 2026). Alizadeh et al. (2026) ran Claude Code and Codex 20 times each on a many-analysts study of immigration and social policy. The agents varied their model specifications at least as much as the human teams had, but their estimates stayed broadly in line with the human consensus, and the authors located the agents' vulnerability in interpretation more than in estimation.

The task in this experiment was far simpler, with two types of prime, participants crossed with words and one obvious family of models. On balanced data, the agents varied only in wording and in secondary choices such as a covariate that could not affect the estimate. On unbalanced data, even the `r count_text(n_distinct(unbalanced_prose$result_line))` different results of the prose replies lay within `r sprintf('%.1f', reply_spread)` ms of one another. Bertran et al. (2026) propose deploying AI analysts against a published specification to reveal how much disagreement comes from underspecified design choices. Here, the open request produced little disagreement to reveal. That consistency belongs to one model on one structured task and may not survive the next update (Chen et al., 2024). The reproducibility of a study cannot rest on it, whereas a script and the record of its environment can be checked.

### Why Direct Experience With R and an IDE Matters

The specified request is where the researcher's knowledge entered the experiment. Writing it required knowing that the data call for crossed random effects, that the choice of random slopes changes the interval (Barr et al., 2013) and that transforming reaction times can change the effects being tested (Lo & Andrews, 2015). It also required knowing R, since the request names the function that fits the model, writes the model in the formula notation of lme4 and gives the call to `confint()` that computes the interval. Interpreting the output required knowing that a singular fit is an estimate on the boundary of the parameter space.

The request also shows the limits of a specification. It fixed a Wald interval, which treats the *t* statistic as normal and is anticonservative with few participants or items (Luke, 2017). I chose it because one function call defines it exactly and so makes the scripts comparable. On the unbalanced data, that choice decided whether the interval excluded zero. An analysis for publication would do better to request Satterthwaite or Kenward–Roger degrees of freedom, as computed in the open-request scripts. None of the `r count_text(nrow(specified_runs))` runs given the specified request mentioned either.

Reading the code is the second point of entry. The scripts in this experiment were between `r min(script_lines)` and `r max(script_lines)` lines long. A researcher who reads R can confirm in a few minutes that a script fits the intended model to the intended rows. Such a reader can also spot a dropped random slope, a silent exclusion of trials or an unplanned transformation, and judge whether each is defensible. Every summary of an open-request script reported dropping the by-participant slope and justified it by the fit of the maximal model. Weighing that justification against the chance that the effect varies across participants in the population, as it does in this simulation, takes knowledge that the summary does not supply. Without experience of R, the researcher is left with the agent's summary of its own work, which is another text generated by the same model.

Research on automation explains why the knowledge needed to specify and read an agent's code has to be maintained. Bainbridge (1983) observed that automation leaves its operators to monitor the system and to take over when it fails, while the skills needed for both decay without practice. Complacency towards automation arises when other tasks compete for attention, occurs in experts as well as novices and is not overcome by simple practice (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010). Impressions of AI assistance can also be wrong. In a randomised trial, 16 experienced open-source developers took 19% longer to complete tasks when allowed AI tools, although they believed afterwards that the tools had cut their time by 20% (Becker et al., 2025). Among 319 knowledge workers surveyed, higher confidence in generative AI was associated with less self-reported critical thinking, and higher self-confidence with more (Lee et al., 2025). Developers who learned a new programming library with AI assistance scored lower on a later test of their understanding of it than those who learned without, and were not significantly faster (Shen & Tamkin, 2026). Messeri and Crockett (2024) warn that AI tools can leave scientists believing that they understand more than they do. For early-career researchers in particular, the ability to check an agent's code has to be built by writing code, and the workflow outlined below depends on that ability.

The checks this experiment needed, from reading each script to comparing its outputs line by line, are what an integrated development environment (IDE) makes routine. An IDE shows a diff of every change, works with version control, displays the objects in memory and can run a script again in a fresh session, which makes it a practical place to work with an agent's code.

### A Reproducible Workflow With Coding Agents

The experiment suggests a workflow in which the project lives under version control, with a lockfile for its packages. The analysis plan is written before the agent writes any code, ideally in a preregistration, so that the request is a specified one. The agent writes scripts into files, and the researcher reads each diff before accepting it, runs the scripts in a fresh session and commits them together with their outputs and a record of the environment. The prompts, the agent's replies and a log of its tool calls are kept beside the scripts. Where possible, the agent's code is first tested on simulated data with known parameters, as pilotr allows, to check that it recovers the effect before it meets real data. Where a model processes the data itself, as in text annotation, it is better to use one whose version can be pinned, such as an open model run locally (Palmer et al., 2024; Spirling, 2023).

### Limitations

The experiment ran on one day, with one model, one version of Claude Code and one simulated data set, on which the lower bound of the interval for the priming effect lay close to zero. With `r count_text(runs_per_cell)` runs in each combination of condition and route, the counts describe these runs and do not estimate rates. The follow-up was designed after the first results. The specified request contained the model formula and the function for the interval, so the agreement among its scripts tested implementation more than analysis. The prose route imitated a chat without a code interpreter, although many chat assistants can now run code. Its agents had no time limit and took up to `r sprintf('%.0f', range_in('prose')[2])` minutes per reply.
